paragraphs: Generating molecular configurations can require substantial computation, especially when using methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo to explore equilibrium states. This paper proposes a probabilistic model that takes a molecule’s graph representation and generates statistically independent samples. The task is to connect the molecule’s structural description with the spatial arrangements that its atoms can take.

The model learns a low-dimensional space that preserves the geometry of local atomic neighborhoods. Its representation is based on Euclidean distance geometry, so distances provide the organizing principle for learning molecular structure. This matters because a compact representation must still retain the local spatial relationships needed to produce useful molecular configurations.

In a new benchmark for molecular conformation generation, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy. They also show how the model can serve as a proposal distribution for importance sampling when computing molecular properties. That application connects configuration generation to downstream estimation: generated samples become inputs to a sampling scheme for calculating quantities of scientific interest.
icml-2020-a-generative-model-for-molecul.tldr: A probabilistic model generates independent molecular configurations from graphs and supports importance sampling for molecular property calculations.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis prediction works backward from a desired molecule to a set of reactants that could produce it. Template-based methods approach this by matching the target against a large collection of reaction patterns. The paper identifies two drawbacks of that approach: matching is computationally expensive, and the collection’s coverage restricts which reactions can be represented.

The proposed G2Gs method instead transforms one molecular graph into several reactant graphs without using reaction templates. It first identifies reaction centers and splits the target graph into intermediate fragments called synthons. A variational graph translation framework then converts those synthons into the final predicted reactants. This separates finding where a reaction occurs from constructing the corresponding starting molecules.

Experiments report improvements of up to 63% in top-1 accuracy over existing template-free approaches. Performance comes close to leading template-based approaches, while the authors report greater scalability and no requirement for domain knowledge. The findings support graph-to-graphs prediction as a competitive way to avoid dependence on an explicit reaction-template collection.
icml-2020-a-graph-to-graphs-framework-fo.tldr: G2Gs predicts reactants by splitting a target molecular graph and translating the resulting fragments into reactant graphs without reaction templates.

paragraphs: Coastal adaptation involves more than predicting physical damage: government decisions interact with residents’ responses as sea levels change. This paper models that interaction as a Markov decision process. The government acts as the decision maker, while nature and residents form the environment with which it interacts. The formulation focuses on the consequences of climate change, particularly sea level rise.

The theoretical analysis compares approaches to infrastructure development through their expected total costs. Within the model, it supports proactive decisions based on detected sea levels over a straightforward strategy that reacts to costs already imposed by nature. The distinction matters because observed environmental conditions can inform investment before the costs driving a reactive policy have materialized.

The authors also provide a scenario planning tool based on deep reinforcement learning. It incorporates different levels of cooperation among government and resident types, alongside NOAA sea level rise projections. Together, the model and tool connect physical scenarios with stakeholder behavior, allowing infrastructure policies to be studied as continuing decisions within a changing social and environmental system.
icml-2020-a-markov-decision-process-mode.tldr: An MDP model supports proactive coastal infrastructure decisions based on sea levels and provides a reinforcement learning tool for exploring adaptation scenarios.

paragraphs: When several probability distributions must be learned from a fixed sampling budget, the central decision is how to divide observations among them. This paper studies allocating samples to a finite collection of discrete distributions so that the largest estimation error is as small as possible. That objective prioritizes learning every distribution reasonably well, rather than achieving a good average while leaving one poorly estimated.

The authors introduce a general optimistic tracking algorithm and compare its allocation with an oracle allocation. They then specialize the framework to four measures of discrepancy: squared L2 distance, L1 distance, f-divergence, and separation distance. The resulting regret bounds describe performance across these different ways of measuring estimation error.

Lower bounds on expected deviation from the oracle show that the algorithm’s allocation performance cannot generally be improved by an adaptive scheme. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The authors also extend their techniques to some continuous distribution classes and to minimizing average error, showing that the allocation framework reaches beyond its original worst-error objective.
icml-2020-adaptive-sampling-for-estimati.tldr: An adaptive sampling framework allocates a fixed budget across distributions, with regret guarantees and lower bounds on tracking an oracle allocation.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning can improve models by pooling data from several parties, but participation depends on whether contributors receive worthwhile rewards. This paper studies a scheme in which each party receives a model as its reward. It values contributions using Shapley value and the information that a party’s data provides about model parameters, connecting reward allocation to the usefulness of contributed data.

The authors define desirable properties, including fairness and stability, drawing on cooperative game theory. Those properties are adapted to an unusual feature of the reward: models can be copied freely. The proposed allocation scheme satisfies fairness and uses an adjustable parameter to trade off among the other desirable properties.

To realize the assigned reward values, the method injects Gaussian noise into the aggregated training data, optimizing the noise variance. This links the abstract allocation of value to the models actually delivered to participants. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets examine the scheme’s properties and performance, illustrating how contribution measurement and model construction can jointly support incentives for collaboration.
icml-2020-collaborative-machine-learning.tldr: A collaborative learning scheme rewards data contributors with models whose values reflect their contributions and adjustable fairness-related tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Gaussian Markov random fields model dependencies across spatial structures and are widely used in spatial statistics. This paper establishes a formal connection between those probabilistic models and convolutional neural networks. Specifically, common GMRFs can be expressed as special cases of a generative model whose mapping from observed data back to latent variables is a single-layer linear CNN.

That connection provides a route to richer models: replace the single convolutional layer with a multilayer architecture. The resulting deep GMRF increases the order of the spatial model while retaining favorable computational scaling. The contribution therefore joins a probabilistic approach to spatial dependence with the compositional structure of convolutional networks.

The authors describe how automatic differentiation and variational inference support efficient learning and inference in the resulting model. On a satellite temperature dataset, they report better prediction and predictive uncertainty than the state of the art. These findings show the practical value of the connection for both estimating spatial quantities and expressing uncertainty about those estimates.
icml-2020-deep-gaussian-markov-random-fi.tldr: A formal connection to convolutional networks enables deeper Gaussian Markov random fields with efficient inference and improved satellite temperature predictions.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning searches a large space of neural-network policies, which can demand substantial amounts of experience. This paper draws on the observation that many continuous-state environments have smooth transitions. It proposes encouraging a corresponding smoothness in the policy, so that small changes in the observed state do not produce unnecessarily abrupt changes in behavior.

The resulting framework, Smooth Regularized Reinforcement Learning, adds smoothness-inducing regularization during policy training. This constrains the space of policies the learner explores while directly shaping how the learned policy responds to nearby states. The same mechanism can improve robustness to state measurement errors, because those errors perturb the inputs on which decisions depend.

The authors apply the framework to TRPO, an on-policy algorithm, and DDPG, an off-policy algorithm. Their experiments report improvements in both sample efficiency and robustness. They also describe a natural extension to a distributionally robust setting. The contribution is a training framework that can strengthen existing learning algorithms by encoding a useful smoothness preference, motivated by the behavior of many continuous environments.
icml-2020-deep-reinforcement-learning-wi.tldr: Smoothness regularization improves sample efficiency and robustness in experiments with both on-policy and off-policy reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A text-generating variational autoencoder can produce useful outputs while leaving the meaning of its latent variables unclear. Mixture priors offer a possible route toward interpretation: different components could correspond to hidden semantic aspects of the text. This paper generalizes Gaussian-mixture VAEs into DEM-VAE, a class of models whose priors are mixtures drawn from the exponential family.

The authors identify a training obstacle: standard variational training suffers from mode collapse, undermining the intended structure of the mixture representation. They provide a theoretical account of the root cause and introduce an additional dispersion term in the training objective. Its purpose is to encourage a structured latent space in which the mixture can fulfill its representational role.

Experiments show that the resulting approach learns a meaningful latent space and outperforms strong baselines on text generation benchmarks. These findings connect interpretability with generation performance: the modification is intended to preserve useful distinctions inside the representation while also supporting high-quality output. The contribution combines a broader model family with a training method designed to address its collapse problem.
icml-2020-dispersed-exponential-family-m.tldr: DEM-VAE uses exponential-family mixture priors and a dispersion penalty to address mode collapse and learn meaningful latent representations for text generation.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from historical observational data is useful when decisions must be improved using existing records. A major difficulty is that the environment producing those records may differ from the environment where the policy will operate. This paper addresses that mismatch in offline contextual bandits, rather than relying on the deployment environment being identical to the historical one.

The authors develop a distributionally robust learning approach aimed at handling adversarial perturbations and unknown shifts in the covariates. They first provide a procedure for evaluating a policy when the environment is ambiguous. That evaluation step makes uncertainty about the future environment part of how a candidate policy is assessed.

They then give a heuristic algorithm for efficiently solving the robust policy learning problem. Extensive simulations demonstrate robustness of the resulting policy. The two components address complementary needs: assessing decisions under environmental uncertainty and searching for a policy that performs robustly under that uncertainty. The findings support the approach in the simulated settings, with the efficient learning procedure explicitly presented as a heuristic.
icml-2020-distributionally-robust-policy.tldr: A distributionally robust approach evaluates and learns offline contextual-bandit policies for environments that may differ from the historical data.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often relies on the Markov assumption: the state used for decision making contains the relevant information from the past. Whether that assumption fits observed data matters for the empirical validity of the resulting model. This paper proposes a Forward-Backward Learning procedure that tests the assumption in sequential decision-making settings, making it an object of statistical investigation.

The test does not require a parametric form for the joint distribution of the observations. This allows the procedure to assess the Markov property without first committing to a particular distributional formula. The authors establish theoretical validity for the test and connect its role to identifying optimal policies in higher-order and partially observable Markov decision processes.

Experiments use both synthetic datasets and an example from mobile health studies to illustrate the test’s usefulness. The central contribution is a way to examine whether a foundational modeling assumption is supported by sequential data. That assessment is relevant when policy learning depends on how the observed history is represented as a state.
icml-2020-does-the-markov-decision-proce.tldr: A theoretically validated Forward-Backward Learning test checks the Markov assumption in sequential decision data without specifying a parametric joint distribution.

paragraphs: Text autoencoders learn sentence representations that could support editing through operations on latent vectors. But successful reconstruction does not necessarily give those vectors a useful arrangement. The paper demonstrates that similar sentences need not be encoded near one another and explains theoretically why high-capacity autoencoders can associate sequences with arbitrary latent representations.

The proposed remedy adds a denoising objective to an adversarial autoencoder. Instead of only reconstructing a sentence from its own representation, the model learns to reconstruct the original sentence from a perturbed version. The authors prove that this modification encourages similar texts to receive similar representations, giving the latent space a more coherent geometry.

In empirical comparisons with several autoencoder types, the resulting DAAE model offers the best reported balance between generation quality and reconstruction capacity. Its improved latent geometry also enables zero-shot text style transfer through simple vector arithmetic. The findings show why the organization of representations matters alongside reconstruction: a space that preserves relationships among texts can support meaningful manipulations of those texts.
icml-2020-educating-text-autoencoders-la.tldr: Adding denoising to adversarial text autoencoders encourages coherent latent geometry and enables zero-shot style transfer through vector arithmetic.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label classification assigns relevant labels to an input from a very large set of possibilities. This paper studies a harder supervision setting: labels are known for groups of examples, but their assignments to individual examples are unavailable. Existing extreme-classification methods do not directly handle this structure, while established multi-instance multi-label methods do not scale to the required label universe.

The authors introduce a scalable algorithm that imputes individual-example labels from the aggregated group labels. Those inferred labels can then be used with any existing extreme multi-label classifier. This creates a bridge between the supervision that is available and the training format that established large-scale classifiers expect.

The paper characterizes the imputation algorithm’s statistical properties under mild assumptions and extends the approach into an end-to-end framework for multi-instance multi-label learning. Experiments on both problem types show advantages over existing approaches. The contribution therefore addresses both compatibility and scale: it makes group-level supervision usable by extreme classifiers and provides a related framework for learning directly in the grouped setting.
icml-2020-extreme-multi-label-classifica.tldr: A scalable label-imputation algorithm turns group-level annotations into training labels usable by existing extreme multi-label classifiers.

paragraphs: Repeatedly sampling from a generative model can return duplicate outputs, which may add little value when the goal is to explore different possibilities. This paper develops sampling without replacement for a broad class of randomized programs. The supported class includes neural generative models that construct their outputs sequentially, so the procedure applies to settings with many possible complete sequences.

The distinctive feature is that sampling is incremental: a user can draw one new sample at a time. The procedure remains efficient even when the output space is exponentially large. Together, these properties support flexible generation of distinct outputs without requiring the sampling process to deliver its entire collection at once.

The authors also introduce an estimator for expectations computed from samples drawn without replacement. This extends the contribution beyond producing diverse outputs to using those samples for numerical estimation. Applications include program synthesis and combinatorial optimization. Across these settings, the shared motivation is to spend sampling effort on new candidates while retaining a method for estimating expectations from the resulting collection.
icml-2020-incremental-sampling-without-r.tldr: An incremental procedure draws distinct outputs from sequential generative models efficiently, with a companion estimator for expectations.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks often base decisions more on local texture than on overall shape. This paper investigates whether reducing that preference can improve robustness across several kinds of challenging conditions. Its motivation is the reported relationship between texture dependence and sensitivity to distribution shifts, image corruption, and adversarial perturbations.

The proposed Informative Dropout method uses local self-information in an image to distinguish texture from shape. A dropout-like procedure then reduces the dependence of the model’s output on local texture. The method is described as lightweight and model-agnostic, with the additional aim of improving interpretability. Its central intervention changes which visual information the model is encouraged to rely on.

Experiments report enhanced robustness in domain generalization, few-shot classification, image corruption, and adversarial perturbation scenarios. These observations support investigating shape bias as a shared route toward several kinds of robustness. The paper’s broad aim is a unified improvement, while its stated evidence is empirical improvement across the evaluated scenarios rather than a guarantee covering every possible disturbance.
icml-2020-informative-dropout-for-robust.tldr: InfoDrop reduces CNN reliance on local texture and empirically improves robustness across several types of challenging visual conditions.

paragraphs: Neural-network loss landscapes can contain disconnected minima and undesirable local minima, yet training often reaches zero training error. This paper examines how stochastic gradient descent and over-parameterization help explain that apparent tension. It proves that solutions found by SGD can be joined by piecewise linear paths whose increase in loss vanishes as the number of neurons becomes large.

The key connection is dropout stability. As networks widen, SGD solutions become increasingly stable to removing some neurons and suitably rescaling those that remain. The resulting change in loss depends on the number of surviving neurons rather than the network’s original total size. This stability supports the construction of paths that connect trained solutions with little additional loss.

The dimensional requirements differ by architecture. For two-layer networks the results are dimension-free, while multilayer networks require neuron counts that scale linearly with input dimension. Numerical experiments across architectures and classification tasks support the theory. The result describes approximate connectivity of SGD solutions as width grows, helping explain favorable optimization behavior without asserting that every minimum is connected.
icml-2020-landscape-connectivity-and-dro.tldr: Increasing network width makes SGD solutions more dropout-stable and connectable by paths whose excess loss vanishes with width.

paragraphs: An autonomous system can affect several users at once, so optimizing its behavior raises questions about how benefits are distributed. This paper formulates a reinforcement learning problem that explicitly seeks equitable treatment of users. It defines a notion of fairness and incorporates that notion into the objective used to learn a policy.

The theoretical analysis considers both discounted rewards and average rewards. It also derives a result for standard reinforcement learning: a bound on the average-reward approximation error of a policy that is optimal for discounted reward. This addresses the relationship between two ways of valuing outcomes over time, which matters because learning with discounted rewards is generally easier.

The analysis further supports using discounted-reward learning to find fair policies for an average-reward objective. The authors show how to adapt several established deep reinforcement learning algorithms to their fairness formulation and validate the approach experimentally in three domains. The contribution combines an explicit fairness objective with a theoretical account of how a more tractable learning formulation can serve a longer-run reward goal.
icml-2020-learning-fair-policies-in-mult.tldr: The paper formalizes fairness in multi-user reinforcement learning and connects discounted-reward learning with fair average-reward objectives.

paragraphs: Dose-finding trials face a difficult tradeoff when a treatment’s efficacy and toxicity do not move together simply. Common approaches focus on identifying a maximum tolerated dose using toxicity events. This paper introduces Safe Efficacy Exploration Dose Allocation, or SEEDA, which instead aims to maximize cumulative efficacy while satisfying a toxicity safety constraint with high probability.

That objective makes outcomes during allocation part of the learning problem, alongside the eventual dose recommendation. The authors evaluate cumulative efficacy, recommendation and allocation success, toxicity-constraint violations, and sample efficiency. They also propose SEEDA-Plateau for molecularly targeted agents whose efficacy increases and then levels off, explicitly adapting the algorithm to that response pattern.

Numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets report that SEEDA finds the optimal dose more successfully and with fewer patients than state-of-the-art trial designs. These findings support the methodology in the evaluated settings. Its safety objective remains probabilistic: the framework seeks high-probability satisfaction of a toxicity constraint while learning which dose offers the best efficacy.
icml-2020-learning-for-dose-allocation-i.tldr: SEEDA adaptively allocates doses to improve cumulative efficacy while targeting high-probability satisfaction of a toxicity constraint.

paragraphs: Group synchronization seeks underlying group elements from measured relationships between them. This paper focuses on rotation synchronization, where the unknown elements are rotations and the measurements describe their relative relationships. The central difficulty is recovering those elements when the measurements contain substantial noise and corruption, so their reliability varies across the available information.

The method combines corruption estimation with reweighted least squares. It begins with a previously developed message passing algorithm that has theoretical guarantees for estimating corruption levels in measured group ratios. Those estimates initialize the weights in the least-squares procedure and guide their updates as the procedure iterates. Reliability assessment is therefore built into the estimation process.

The authors present the resulting algorithm as an efficient approach to synchronization under heavy corruption and noise. Experiments on synthetic and real rotation data demonstrate better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is the coupling of message-passing estimates of measurement quality with an iterative fitting procedure, allowing the inferred corruption levels to influence the recovery of the underlying rotations.
icml-2020-message-passing-least-squares-.tldr: Message-passing estimates of measurement corruption guide reweighted least squares for robust rotation synchronization.

paragraphs: This paper studies adaptive control of a linear quadratic regulator when the system parameters are unknown. The learner must control the system while gathering information about its dynamics. Matching upper and lower bounds show that optimal regret scales as the square root of d_u squared times d_x times T, up to logarithmic factors, where the dimensions describe controls and states.

The upper bound comes from a simple certainty-equivalent strategy: act using the optimal controller for the current estimated system and add exploratory random noise. Continually refining the system estimates makes this approach optimal in its dependence on dimension as well as time. The lower bounds also rule out regret that grows only polynomially in log T, resolving the conjectured possibility described in the paper.

A new self-bounding ODE method controls perturbations of Riccati equations, linking errors in estimated dynamics to controller suboptimality. This analysis supports upper bounds for any stabilizable instance, with dependence on natural control-theoretic quantities. The result gives a precise theoretical justification for a simple exploration strategy.
icml-2020-naive-exploration-is-optimal-f.tldr: Certainty-equivalent control with random exploration and continually refined estimates achieves optimal time and dimension dependence for online LQR regret.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit, earlier rewards influence which options are sampled later, so ordinary sample averages can become biased. This paper studies an additional complication: an average may be examined only when some event occurs. Bias across all runs and bias among the selected runs answer different questions, and results about the former need not determine the latter.

The authors characterize the direction of conditional bias for monotone functions of rewards, including sample means. Their results allow arbitrary conditioning events and use natural monotonicity properties of the data collection policy. This connects the selection event and the policy’s response to data with whether the reported statistic tends to be too high or too low.

Examples from sequential testing and best-arm identification show that conditional and marginal bias can have different signs. A statistic biased upward overall can therefore behave differently within a selected subset of runs, depending on the conditioning event. The contribution clarifies why bias assessments in adaptive studies must account for the conditions under which a result is examined.
icml-2020-on-conditional-versus-marginal.tldr: The paper characterizes conditional bias in adaptive bandit data and shows that its direction can differ from overall bias.

paragraphs: Distributed ridge regression allows separate machines to fit estimators on their data and then combine the results. This paper studies one-shot methods that form a weighted combination of those local estimators. The question is how to choose the combination well when the data are high-dimensional, so that distributing the computation remains statistically effective.

The analysis examines mean squared error in a model where each predictor has a small effect. Within that setting, efficiency depends strongly on signal strength but does not deteriorate with many workers, and the risk separates across machines. Another finding is that the optimal combination weights do not sum to one, so the best combination is not a conventional weighted average.

Using these results, the authors propose an optimally weighted one-shot ridge regression algorithm. Simulations and real-data analysis support their findings. The contribution shows that aggregation deserves its own statistical design: local estimators can be combined more effectively by accounting for signal strength and the structure of the high-dimensional risk.
icml-2020-one-shot-distributed-ridge-reg.tldr: High-dimensional risk analysis yields an optimally weighted distributed ridge estimator whose weights need not sum to one.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation in the network’s representation. Building that property into image networks is difficult because images and feature maps occupy discrete grids, which support only limited transformation groups exactly. This paper approaches the problem through the relationship between convolutions and partial differential operators.

Assuming smooth inputs, the authors construct a system equivariant to the continuous n-dimensional Euclidean group. They then discretize that system using numerical schemes for differential operators, producing PDO-eConvs. The implemented convolutions are approximately equivariant, and the paper provides an error analysis showing a quadratic-order approximation error. This distinguishes the continuous theoretical property from what survives numerical implementation.

Experiments on rotated MNIST and natural image classification report competitive performance with much greater parameter efficiency. In the stated comparison with Wide ResNets, the method performs better while using only 12.6% as many parameters. The findings support differential operators as a practical way to incorporate broader geometric structure into convolutional architectures while quantifying the approximation introduced by the grid.
icml-2020-pdo-econvs-partial-differentia.tldr: PDO-eConvs discretize a continuously equivariant differential-operator system into parameter-efficient convolutions with quantified approximate equivariance.

paragraphs: Piecewise linear regression represents a relationship using linear pieces that can accommodate changes in behavior across the input space. This paper constructs such an estimate as the difference between two convex functions. Each component is itself piecewise linear, fitted in a manner related to max-affine regression, and their difference is used to approximate the observed data.

The method introduces a seminorm to regularize this class of difference-of-convex functions. That regularizer controls the estimate’s Lipschitz constant in the infinity norm, providing a way to constrain how sharply its predictions can change. The representation and regularization work together to balance flexibility with control over the fitted function’s variation.

The resulting fitting procedure can be implemented efficiently through quadratic programming, including in high dimensions. The authors establish statistical risk close to the minimax benchmark and empirically demonstrate practical implementation. On real-world datasets, they report greater accuracy than existing regression methods. The contribution combines a flexible function representation, a regularizer with a clear mathematical role, and a tractable optimization procedure.
icml-2020-piecewise-linear-regression-vi.tldr: Fitting a regularized difference of piecewise linear convex functions yields efficient regression with near-minimax statistical risk.

paragraphs: Transformers for language typically use layer normalization, whereas batch normalization is common in computer vision. This paper investigates why applying ordinary batch normalization to language transformers often degrades performance. Its systematic study finds large fluctuations in statistics across the batch dimension throughout training, which create instability when batch normalization is used naively.

Power Normalization addresses this in three linked ways. It relaxes the requirement to normalize activations to zero mean, replaces individual-batch statistics with a running quadratic mean, and uses approximate backpropagation to accommodate running statistics in the forward computation. These changes target the fluctuating quantities identified by the study rather than simply transplanting the standard batch-normalization procedure.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that Power Normalization gives the loss a smaller Lipschitz constant than batch normalization. They also prove bounded gradients for the approximate backpropagation scheme. Experiments across transformer language tasks report significant improvements over both layer and batch normalization, including gains in translation BLEU and language-model perplexity. The theoretical and empirical results jointly support the revised normalization design.
icml-2020-powernorm-rethinking-batch-nor.tldr: PowerNorm stabilizes batch-based normalization in language transformers using running quadratic statistics and approximate backpropagation, improving evaluated NLP performance.

paragraphs: Controlling a system from high-dimensional observations is challenging when its dynamics are unknown. Learning Controllable Embedding methods address this by compressing observations, learning dynamics in the latent space, and controlling the system there. Existing approaches also reconstruct the next observation to ensure that the learned dynamics retain predictive information, requiring a decoder that is later discarded during control.

This paper develops an information-theoretic approach and shows theoretically that predictive coding can replace explicit prediction in the original observation space. The authors use that result to construct a decoder-free model. Its latent dynamics are designed to support locally linear control, connecting the learned representation directly to the requirements of the control procedure.

Experiments on benchmark tasks show that the model reliably learns a controllable latent space and outperforms state-of-the-art LCE baselines. The contribution removes the need to solve a high-dimensional reconstruction task as part of learning a useful control representation. Its theoretical replacement and empirical results support learning predictive latent dynamics without maintaining the extra decoder parameters.
icml-2020-predictive-coding-for-locally-.tldr: Predictive coding replaces explicit next-observation reconstruction in a decoder-free latent model that supports locally linear control.
